summary: Gives guidance on how to use Internet PKI certificates to carry Key Exchange Algorithm (KEA) keys. It is informational.

eli5.summary: This explains how to put one particular kind of secret-code key into a digital ID card so others can use it.

subtitle: How to encode Key Exchange Algorithm keys inside standard X.509 digital certificates.

tldr.problem: The Key Exchange Algorithm (KEA) is a classified algorithm used for key exchange, but X.509 certificates lack a standardized way to carry KEA public keys and their associated parameters.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC profiles how to place a KEA public key in the subjectPublicKey field of an X.509 V3 certificate, specifies the algorithm identifier and parameter encoding, and defines which key usage extensions are permitted.
tldr.outcome: Systems that need to use KEA keys can now encode them in standard X.509 certificates following a consistent format, enabling interoperability among implementations in communities using this algorithm.

today: RFC 2528 is an Informational RFC that profiles KEA key representation in X.509 certificates. It is a technical specification for communities using the KEA algorithm and remains valid for that purpose.

sections.title: KEA and X.509 Certificates
sections.content:
The Key Exchange Algorithm (KEA) is a classified cryptographic algorithm for exchanging secret keys between two parties. It generates a shared pairwise key when two entities have KEA public keys created with the same parameters. To use KEA in real systems, implementations need a standard way to store and distribute KEA public keys.

X.509 V3 certificates are the standard vehicle for distributing public keys on the Internet. This RFC extends RFC 2459 (the Internet PKI certificate profile) to specify exactly how to represent KEA keys in X.509 certificates, covering the placement of the key in the certificate, the algorithm identifier, parameter encoding, and the allowed key usage extensions.
sections.eli5: KEA is a secret-key exchange method. This document explains how to pack a KEA key into a digital ID card so that different computer programs all understand how to read and use it.

sections.title: Subject Public Key Info and Algorithm Identifier
sections.content:
A KEA public key is placed in the subjectPublicKey field of an X.509 certificate as a BIT STRING. The key is encoded with its most significant bit as the first bit of the string and its least significant bit as the last.

The certificate identifies the KEA algorithm through an algorithm identifier consisting of an object identifier (OID) and parameters. The OID for KEA is { 2 16 840 1 101 2 1 1 22 }. Unlike other algorithms, KEA parameters are not embedded in the certificate itself. Instead, the parameters field contains an 80-bit domain identifier (OCTET STRING), which uniquely identifies the set of KEA parameters that were used to generate the key.

The domain identifier is computed in three steps: (1) the KEA parameters are DER-encoded, (2) a 160-bit SHA-1 hash is computed over the encoded parameters, and (3) the hash is reduced to 80 bits by XORing the high-order 80 bits with the low-order 80 bits. This compact identifier allows certificates to reference parameter sets without storing the full parameters.
sections.eli5: The key is stored as a long number in the certificate. The certificate also includes a small code (80 bits) that identifies which parameter set was used to make the key, computed by hashing and shrinking the parameters.

sections.title: Key Usage Extension for KEA Certificates
sections.content:
The X.509 key usage extension specifies what operations a public key is allowed to be used for. For KEA certificates, only three values are permitted: keyAgreement (the key can be used to establish shared secrets), encipherOnly (the key can encrypt but not decrypt), and decipherOnly (the key can decrypt but not encrypt).

The encipherOnly and decipherOnly values may only be asserted if keyAgreement is also asserted. At most one of encipher-only and decipher-only can be set. In the typical case, only keyAgreement is asserted without either of the directional modifiers.
sections.eli5: The certificate can say what the key is allowed to do: help two people agree on a secret, encrypt messages, or decrypt messages. You cannot restrict it too much, and you can usually just say it is for agreement.

sections.title: ASN.1 Module Definition
sections.content:
The RFC provides the formal definition of the KEA algorithm and parameters in ASN.1 notation, the notation used to define data structures in X.509 certificates. Two versions are given: one using 1988 syntax and one using 1993 syntax, for compatibility with different certificate libraries.

Both versions define the same two elements: the OID for the algorithm and the type definition for the parameters (a simple OCTET STRING). This allows certificate libraries to recognize and process KEA keys correctly regardless of the internal representation used by the implementation.
sections.eli5: The document includes the formal machine-readable definition of the KEA algorithm so that programming libraries can automatically parse and validate certificates containing KEA keys.
